headline: Shipbuilders in South Korea, Japan and Singapore are racing to put data centres on the sea to get around shortages of land and power for AI, though whether they will pay is unproven.
score_reason: Pool 4 kept: the full article was read; it is a survey of early projects and plans with no first unit running yet, and the economics are unproven.
importance_line: What changed is that shipbuilders are moving from studies to real builds, which matters first to places short of land and power for data centres, then to AI companies and the shipbuilders, and the doubt is that the first units are due to start only in 2027 and 2028 and Chosunbiz says their cost and stability at sea are still unproven.
summary: Chosunbiz reports that shipbuilders in Singapore, Japan and South Korea are leading a race to build floating data centres, which need no large plots of land and can cool servers with seawater: Singapore's Keppel has begun building a 25-megawatt unit due to start in 2028, the Japanese shipping line MOL is converting secondhand ships with Hitachi, and Samsung Heavy Industries is pursuing a main contract for a 50-megawatt unit with the US developer M3. Chosunbiz says the economics still appear unproven because there is no standard design, costs are high and servers must run reliably amid salt, humidity and waves, and a shipbuilding official says the test is whether they can match the stability and use rate of land-based sites.
notes: Read in full (fulltext). Plans and targets are company statements relayed by Chosunbiz.
